question: How does Ravel make repeated notes carry both pulse and melody?
intro: Repeated notes and rapid exchanges between the hands drive the suite’s finale towards E major. This selection combines different pianists and omits the fourth movement, the Rigaudon; it is not a complete performance of the suite.

sections.label: Repeated-note motion
sections.mNote: The hands alternate rapid attacks around a repeated-note figure.

sections.label: Broader melodic line
sections.mNote: Longer melodic shapes become prominent above the continuing motion.

sections.label: Middle working
sections.mNote: Short figures and broader lines continue to interact.

sections.label: Final drive
sections.mNote: The keyboard writing expands towards the emphatic E-major ending.

cues.title: One note, many attacks
cues.text: The opening’s repeated notes are distributed between the hands. Listen for a continuous pulse rather than two separate streams: the pianist must make those alternating attacks sound connected while keeping the marked staccato clear.
cues.evidence: Durand 1918 piano score, printed p. 24: Vif, 2/4, pp repeated semiquavers shared between the hands and marked with staccato dots. The cue explains the written mechanism, not a precise hand movement at a timestamp.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Remembering Joseph de Marliave
cues.text: The Toccata is dedicated to Captain Joseph de Marliave, killed in the First World War. His name appears above the suite’s most overtly virtuosic finale. The rapid notes belong to a memorial, even though they do not imitate a funeral procession.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 24, dedication to “Capitaine Joseph de Marliave”; BnF dedication list https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb13917720k. The wartime deaths are documented in the Lyon programme: https://www.auditorium-lyon.com/en/node/13646.

cues.title: The opening gains force
cues.text: The quiet repeated-note writing can generate a much larger dynamic without abandoning its rapid pulse. This passage reaches a strong early crest. Hear the growth as an increase of weight and range, not simply as an instruction to play faster.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ravel-tombeau-toccata.txt: loudness rises from −17.6 dB at 55 seconds to −11.7 at 60 and −7.7 at 65, then recedes. Durand score, pp. 25–27, expands the keyboard texture; no tempo measurement is inferred from loudness.

cues.title: The widow at the piano
cues.text: Marguerite Long, de Marliave’s widow, gave the first performance of the complete piano suite at the Salle Gaveau in Paris on 11 April 1919. The pianist who introduced the work was therefore directly connected to the person remembered in its final movement.
cues.evidence: BnF documents the complete-suite premiere, date, venue and pianist: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb13917720k. Susan Halpern’s Celebrity Series programme, 18 November 2018, PDF p. 4, identifies the Toccata’s dedicatee as Long’s late husband: https://celebrity-series.s3.amazonaws.com/files/resources/1913a-inon-barnatan-notes-for-web.pdf.

cues.title: Melody above the mechanism
cues.text: The rapid notes are not the whole argument. Ravel also writes longer melodic spans, which the pianist must bring forward without letting the underlying movement become heavy. Try following that broader line across several beats rather than counting every attack.
cues.evidence: Durand score, printed pp. 27–29, longer melodic values and phrasing against active accompaniment. The cue is a middle-passage listening task; it does not claim a newly entering theme at 120 seconds.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Meyer’s Paris recording
cues.text: This performance comes from Marcelle Meyer’s Paris sessions at the Salle Adyar, dated 5–8 March 1954 in the source credit. The Commons file points to Les Discophiles Français, catalogue DF 100/1. The much later digital upload is not the recording date.
cues.evidence: Selected Commons file, author and source credits: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Maurice_Ravel_-_Le_Tombeau_de_Couperin_-_Toccata_(Marcelle_Meyer).flac. The source identifies the session range, venue and catalogue; it does not assign this track to an individual day.

cues.title: A sustained late climb
cues.text: The final stretch becomes louder and stays forceful for longer than the earlier crest. Follow the accumulating weight across successive phrases: Ravel is building an ending, not inserting one isolated loud chord into the repeated-note texture.
cues.evidence: Analysis rises from −12.2 dB at 175 seconds to −7.1 at 180 and −4.4 at 185; windows from 185 to 225 remain markedly strong, with the loudest at 195. Durand score, pp. 30–32, enlarges the final piano writing.

cues.title: Ending in E major
cues.text: The movement that began in E minor closes in E major. The last page makes the change concrete with a four-sharp key signature and emphatic chords. Listen to the final repeated attacks as part of that harmonic arrival, not merely as a last display of speed.
cues.evidence: Durand score, printed p. 32, E-major key signature and final E-major chord. The analysis places sustained high energy through the 215–225-second windows and decay after 230. This locates the final page broadly, not the exact modulation.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A line above the attacks
transitions.how: The motor rhythm does not have to stop for a more sustained melody to become audible. Ravel changes the balance of the piano texture: longer upper notes and their phrasing ask for attention above the rapid accompaniment. The join changes what the listener follows rather than replacing the instrument or metre.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, pp. 27–29, contrasts running figures with longer melodic spans. Analysis has its strongest boundary candidate at 86 seconds and lower detected attack density around 85–105. This is an approximate passage division, not a bar-aligned thematic entry.

transitions.title: The two kinds of motion interact
transitions.how: Short repeated figures and the broader line continue to share the keyboard. Register and dynamic changes redistribute the emphasis between them. The connection depends on material already heard, so the movement can renew its activity without making a clean break or announcing a new tempo.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, pp. 28–30, develops the contrasting types of figuration. Analysis candidates at 126 and 132 seconds support a broad listening division; no exact sonata-form boundary or thematic return is asserted.

transitions.title: The piano fills out
transitions.how: The late crescendo broadens the keyboard texture and prepares the E-major close. Repeated attacks remain an organising force, now reinforced by fuller chords and a stronger bass. Rather than interrupting the motion with a cadenza, Ravel drives it into the final harmonic arrival.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, pp. 30–32, final expansion and E-major conclusion. Analysis boundary candidate at 188 seconds lies within the rise from −12.2 dB at 175 to −3.3 at 195; the exact change into E major is not timed.

composer.epithet: An engineer of instrumental colour who made a piano imitate water, an orchestra imitate a machine, and old dances carry the names of the dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; composition with Fauré from 1897, counterpoint with André Gedalge
Les Apaches: Ricardo Viñes, Maurice Delage, Tristan Klingsor, Michel-Dimitri Calvocoressi and other musicians, writers and painters
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum preserving his piano and collections
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber music and piano works; no symphony

quote.source: Ravel, as remembered by his friend M. D. Calvocoressi

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.
